notes:
I've gathered material from multiple sources across traditions. Let me now compile the verse-by-verse notes.

---

# 2 Chronicles 9 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

Matthew Henry notes that this chapter closely parallels 1 Kings 10, but the Chronicler deliberately **omits Solomon's later defection** (recorded in 1 Kings 11), bringing him "to the grave with an unstained reputation." The Pulpit Commentary says the writer "is about to take his leave of Solomon and the glowing memories of his golden reign" and does so "in a most dramatically successful manner." Precept Austin (citing Andrew Hill) observes that the chapter "balances the opening chapter (ch. 1) in that God has honored Solomon's obedience in giving the wealth accumulated by David to the building of the temple by restoring wealth to the monarchy through trade and gifts from other nations." (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC14009.HTM; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-9.html; https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-9-commentary)

---

## v. 1 — The Queen of Sheba Arrives

**Sheba** is identified with ancient Saba, in the region of modern Yemen (Southern Arabia), about 1,400–1,500 miles from Jerusalem. The Pulpit Commentary discusses whether Sheba was Cushite, Joktanite, or Jokshanite in origin and notes it was "reputed splendid, the country wealthy." Sheba was famous for spices and trading skill, and extrabiblical sources attest that it had female rulers. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-9.html; https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-9-commentary)

Enduring Word notes this was "a long trip – up to about 1,500 miles (2,400 kilometers)" and that "she probably came as part of a trade delegation." Raymond Dillard (cited by Precept Austin) argues that **commercial interests were the more basic motivation**: Sheba's economy was built on frankincense and myrrh trade, and Solomon's naval operations to the south (2 Chr 8:17–18) may have been cutting into her overland routes. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-9/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-9-commentary)

The **"difficult questions"** (Hebrew *khee-DAW*) are literally "riddles, enigmas" (LXX: αἰνίγμασιν). The Pulpit Commentary says these were "enigmas and primitive casuistry, in which the Arabians found some considerable portion of their mental gymnastics." Enduring Word (citing Wiseman) adds: "The hard questions were not just riddles, but included difficult diplomatic and ethical questions." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-9.html; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-9/)

Matthew Henry draws a spiritual application: "Those who know the worth of true wisdom will grudge no pains nor cost to obtain it." (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC14009.HTM)

**Ellicott** notes that the Chronicler substituted "gold in abundance" (a favourite expression) for the "very much gold" of Kings, and that the phrase "at Jerusalem" is "an abridgment but not an improvement of Kings." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/9.htm)

---

## v. 2 — Solomon Answers All Her Questions

The Pulpit Commentary: "Nothing hid from Solomon — i.e. nothing obscure to him—no question knotty for Solomon." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-9.html)

Precept Austin (citing Ron Daniel) notes that after Solomon demonstrated his wisdom, "she opened up and began to speak with him about all that was on her heart," and applies it: "The world is even more desperate now to open up their hearts to those who have wisdom from God." F.B. Meyer is quoted: "Bring your hard questions to Christ; He is greater than Solomon." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-9-commentary)

**Gill** simply refers the reader to the parallel in 1 Kings 10:1. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/9.htm)

---

## vv. 3–4 — The Queen Is Overwhelmed

The Pulpit Commentary discusses the list of seven things the queen saw. Regarding "the meat of his table," it suggests this refers to "the set-out of one meal-table" — the "abounding lading of the table," the variety of courses, rich fruits, and "furnishing and decorating of the table." The "sitting of his servants" and "attendance of his ministers" are difficult to interpret precisely; the Pulpit Commentary considers and dismisses Murphy's view that it refers to the servants "sitting in council." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-9.html)

The **"ascent by which he went up into the house of the LORD"** — the Pulpit Commentary notes this seems "unseasonably" placed among the banquet descriptions but suggests the algum wood terraces/stairs mentioned later (v. 11) may hold a clue to this reference. The LXX reads "the burnt offerings which he offered at the house of the Lord." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-9.html)

**"There was no more spirit in her"** — Enduring Word (citing Clarke) says: "What happened to the queen of Sheba is a natural and not an uncommon effect which will be produced in a delicate sensible mind at the sight of rare and extraordinary productions of art." Matthew Henry says the queen "was exceedingly affected to see the propriety with which Solomon's servants attended him and with which both he and they attended in the house of God." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-9/; https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC14009.HTM)

**Precept Austin** (citing Frederick Mabie) notes the spices were "prized possessions" used in "cosmetics, embalming, religious offerings, and pharmacopeia." Frankincense was an ingredient in the altar of incense (Ex 30:34), and myrrh in the sacred anointing oil (Ex 30:23). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-9-commentary)

---

## vv. 5–6 — "The Half Was Not Told Me"

Enduring Word: "The queen of Sheba heard wonderful things about Solomon and his kingdom, but upon seeing it with her own eyes she realized it was far greater than she had heard." Matthew Henry simply notes she "thought herself well paid for her pains." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-9/; https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC14009.HTM)

---

## v. 7 — "Happy Are Your Men"

Enduring Word: "It is a joyful thing to serve a great, wise, and rich king. If it was a happy thing to serve Solomon, it is a much happier thing to serve Jesus." Matthew Henry notes that "the posterity of those who had places in his court were willing to have the names of their ancestors forgotten, and thought themselves sufficiently distinguished and dignified when they were called the children of Solomon's servants (Ezra 2:55; Neh. 7:57)." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-9/; https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC14009.HTM)

**Grant's Commentary** (Brethren/typological): The queen's delight "looks forward to the day when the Lord Jesus is manifested in His glory... God will so work in the hearts of redeemed Gentiles then that they will have no more attitude of enmity toward Israel, but genuine delight in her exaltation!" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/2-chronicles-9.html)

---

## v. 8 — "Blessed Be the LORD Your God"

This verse is the theological crux of the queen's speech and receives significant attention across traditions.

**Enduring Word** (Pentecostal/charismatic): Raises the question whether this was "a true confession of faith, expressing allegiance to the God of Israel." It suggests these words "may not be more than the queen's response to the astonishing blessing evident in Solomon's Jerusalem," citing Dilday: "Her statement about the blessings of the Lord on Israel and Solomon in verse 8 were no more than a polite reference to Solomon's God" and Wiseman: "Praise to the LORD implies recognition of Israel's national God and need not necessarily be an expression of personal faith." The application: "If we take the queen of Sheba as an example of a seeker, we see that Solomon impressed her with his wealth and splendor... But she returned home without an evident expression of faith in the God of Israel. This shows that impressing seekers with facilities and programs and organization and professionalism isn't enough." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-9/)

**The Pulpit Commentary** (older Protestant): "The abstinence on the part of the queen in her mention of the Lord God of Israel, and of the Lord thy God, of any indication of a desire that he should become her God, is as suggestive as it is noticeable (compare Hiram's language in 2 Chronicles 2:12)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-9.html)

**Matthew Henry** (evangelical): Takes a more positive view — "We ought to rejoice and give God thanks for the gifts, graces, and usefulness, of others. The queen of Sheba blessed God for the honour he put upon Solomon... By giving God the praise of the prosperity of others, we share in the comfort of it." He adds: "The happiness of both king and kingdom she traces up to the fountain of all bliss, the divine favour: it was because thy God delighted in thee and because he loved Israel." (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC14009.HTM)

**Ligonier (Reformed):** Notes that "as God had promised, Abraham's descendants were blessing the world (Gen. 12:1–3)" and that "Solomon's reign shows us that God is not opposed to richly blessing His people. Although great riches and fame are not guaranteed to God's people, neither are they inherently incompatible with faithful service to Him." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/solomons-accomplishments-and-renown)

**Precept Austin** (citing Andrew Hill): The queen "bears witness to the fact that Solomon's wisdom and wealth are the result of God's blessing on the king and his love for the nation of Israel." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-9-commentary)

**Enduring Word** (citing Poole): The statement "He made you king over them" is "especially meaningful because Solomon was not necessarily the most logical successor of his father David. There were several sons of David born before Solomon. 'It was God's special act to make him king rather than his elder brother.'" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-9/)

**Grant's Commentary** (Brethren typological): "Solomon's throne is the throne of the LORD... Thus, the reign of the Lord Jesus over Israel will be a special proof of God's love for His earthly people. At the same time this is a beautiful picture of God's love for the church. God so loves the church that He gave the Lord Jesus, in His capacity as Head over all things, to her (Ephesians 1:22)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/2-chronicles-9.html)

---

## v. 9 — The Queen's Gifts

**The Pulpit Commentary** calculates the value of 120 talents of gold at £4 per ounce: one talent = £5,476, making a total of £657,120 (1880 values). It notes Poole makes it £1,250,000 and S. Clarke £720,000. It also observes: "Much of all this so-termed giving was evidently matter of exchange. The queen got quid pro quo." The Arabian spices and their lucrative trade "are often alluded to by historians (see, among many others, Herodotus, 3:113; Diodorus, 3:46; Strabo, 16:4, §19)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-9.html)

**Precept Austin** (citing Andrew Hill): These aromatic resins "were prized possessions and enjoyed wide use in the biblical world in cosmetics, embalming, religious offerings, and pharmacopeia." Frankincense was used in the altar of incense (Ex 30:34), and myrrh in the sacred anointing oil (Ex 30:23). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-9-commentary)

---

## vv. 10–11 — Algum Wood

**The Pulpit Commentary** suggests these verses may be "misplaced" or may have "some occult bearing on the queen" — the terraces, stairs, or balustrades made of the algum wood "were the artificial-work wonders which helped to astound the queen." It suggests the algum/almug wood may be red sandalwood and notes Max Muller's statement that the vernacular for this wood in India is *valguka*. The wood was used for "walkways" (or terraces/stairs) for the temple and palace, and for harps and psalteries. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-9.html)

---

## v. 12 — Solomon's Generosity to the Queen

Enduring Word: "Solomon would not allow the queen of Sheba to give him more than he gave back to her. This description of Solomon's measure of generosity to the queen of Sheba also describes the measure of God's generosity towards us." It notes that "according to tradition – fanciful stories, perhaps – the queen of Sheba wanted a son by Solomon, and he obliged her. Her child was named Menilek, and he became the ancestor of all subsequent Ethiopian monarchs." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-9/)

Matthew Henry: "They both knew how to value wisdom, and therefore were neither of them covetous of their money... Our Lord Jesus has promised to give us all our desire: Ask, and it shall be given you." (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC14009.HTM)

**Grant's Commentary** (Brethren): "The Queen of Sheba was not impoverished by her giving to Solomon, just as believers today do not suffer lack because they give to the Lord... the Lord will always give us much more than we give to Him." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/2-chronicles-9.html)

---

## vv. 13–14 — Solomon's Yearly Income: 666 Talents

**Enduring Word** devotes significant attention to the number 666. It estimates the value at $1,019,565,360 (2016 gold prices). It notes that "this makes him one of the only two people in the Bible associated with the number 666" — the other being the Antichrist (Revelation 13:18). It suggests: "This isn't to say that Solomon was the Antichrist... But it may indicate that the Antichrist may not be someone purely evil from the very beginning. Instead, he may be like Solomon – a good man corrupted." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-9/)

Enduring Word also notes the subtle warning: "The writer of Chronicles gave a subtle warning signal here. He assumed his readers knew the instructions for future kings of Israel in Deuteronomy 17:14-20... nor shall he greatly multiply silver and gold for himself. God blessed Solomon with great riches, but Solomon allowed that blessing to turn into a danger because he disobediently multiplied silver and gold for himself." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-9/)

**The Pulpit Commentary** notes that the gold "probably came by way of tax payments from the merchant travellers, and as tribute money from the kings" of Arabia and governors of adjacent countries. It gives linguistic details on the unusual word for "governors" (*pachot*), noting it is used in Persian, Chaldean, and Assyrian contexts. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-9.html)

---

## vv. 15–16 — Golden Shields

Enduring Word: "These shields made beautiful displays in the House of the Forest of Lebanon, but they were of no use in battle. Gold was too heavy and too soft to be used as a metal for effective shields. This shows Solomon had the image of a warrior king, but without the substance." It values them at over $53 million total (2016 prices). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-9/)

**The Pulpit Commentary** suggests the "shekel" may actually be the *beka* (half-shekel), making the gold plating more moderate. It notes that Shishak took these shields when he conquered Jerusalem (1 Kings 14:26). The "house of the forest of Lebanon" is identified as an armoury. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-9.html)

---

## vv. 17–19 — The Ivory Throne

**The Pulpit Commentary** discusses whether the throne was solid ivory (cf. Psalm 45:9; Amos 3:15; 6:4) or overlaid, noting the parallel in 1 Kings 10:19 says "the top of the throne was round behind." It notes the lions are "as natural a symbol as it is an old one of sovereign power and place" and the use of twelve lions "reminding of the tribes of Israel, were specifically justified to the people, whose oracles contained such words as those in Genesis 49:9; Numbers 23:24; 24:9." Josephus claimed a golden bull supported the seat — "If so, it is remarkable that the statement should be omitted in both of our Old Testament narrations." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-9.html)

Matthew Henry: "The lustre wherein he appeared was typical of the spiritual glory of the kingdom of the Messiah and but a faint representation of his throne, which is above every throne. Solomon's pomp was all artificial; and therefore our Saviour prefers the natural beauty of the lilies of the field before it (Matt. 6:29)." (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC14009.HTM)

**Clarke's Commentary** (accessed via studylight.org) mentions Jewish and Islamic traditions about the throne involving "preternatural agency in the construction." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-chronicles-9.html)

---

## v. 20 — Gold Vessels; Silver as Nothing

Enduring Word: "This was a statement of wealth. If taken seriously, it shows the tremendous abundance of Solomon's kingdom. Truly, King Solomon surpassed all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom, and the promises of Deuteronomy 28:1-14 were fulfilled in his reign." The Pulpit Commentary notes the connection between the drinking vessels and the "house of the forest of Lebanon," inferring the house's use "for social or, at any rate, state occasions." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-9/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-9.html)

---

## v. 21 — Ships of Tarshish

**The Pulpit Commentary** provides extensive discussion. Tarshish (subsequent Tartessus) "covered a district in South Spain, as well as named a town and river, and stretched opposite the coast of Africa. Both coasts were beneath Phoenician rule, and a voyage to Tarshish would most naturally mean calling at many a port." It discusses whether voyages circumnavigated Africa and consumed three years. The Hebrew names for "ivory, apes, and peacocks" have been claimed to be of Indian (Sanscrit/Tamil) origin, but the Pulpit Commentary pushes back, noting possible Egyptian and African etymologies as well. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-9.html)

---

## vv. 22–23 — Solomon's International Fame

Enduring Word: "This was another fulfillment of the promises of Deuteronomy 28... And the LORD will make you the head and not the tail." Matthew Henry: "Herein he was a type of Christ, to whom, as soon as he was born, the wise men of the east brought presents, gold, frankincense, and myrrh (Matt. 2:11)." He adds a solemn application: "The application which they then made to Solomon to hear his wisdom will aggravate, shame, and condemn, men's general contempt of Christ and his gospel. Though in them are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, yet none of the princes of this world desire to know them, for they are foolishness to them (1 Cor. 2:8, 14)." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-9/; https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC14009.HTM)

**Precept Austin** (citing Martin Selman): "God himself is twice acknowledged as the source of Solomon's gifts, on both occasions through the impartial testimony of foreigners (v. 8, v. 23)." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-9-commentary)

**Ligonier (Reformed):** "God's purpose for Israel was that His people should draw the nations to Yahweh (Exodus 19:5-6). We see Israel realizing this purpose partially in this queen's visit... Other Gentile nations also contributed greatly to Solomon's wealth. God brought this wealth to Solomon because of his obedience. Nevertheless, Solomon only partially fulfilled God's promises. Their complete fulfillment awaited the appearance of the perfectly obedient Son of David." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/solomons-accomplishments-and-renown)

---

## vv. 24–25 — Tribute and Military Resources

**The Pulpit Commentary** notes the Hebrew for "present" is *minchah*, representing "treats, paid partly in money, partly in kind." It clarifies that 2 Chronicles 9:25 says "four thousand stalls" (not forty thousand as in 1 Kings 4:26, which it calls an "error"). The parallel mentions 1,400 chariots (2 Chr 1:14). Both agree on 12,000 horsemen. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-9.html)

---

## v. 26 — Extent of Solomon's Dominion

**Gill** notes this verse is "the same with 1 Kings 4:21" rather than the 1 Kings 10 parallel. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/9.htm)

---

## v. 27 — Silver as Common as Stones

Enduring Word observes: "When we think of Solomon's great wealth, we also consider that he originally did not set his heart upon riches. He deliberately asked for wisdom to lead the people of God instead of riches or fame. God promised to also give Solomon riches and fame, and God fulfilled His promise." It adds: "Solomon gave an eloquent testimony to the vanity of riches as the preacher in the Book of Ecclesiastes. He powerfully showed that there was no ultimate satisfaction through materialism. We don't have to be as rich as Solomon to learn the same lesson." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-9/)

The Pulpit Commentary adds: "The foundations of the evil of exceeding metropolitan centralization were being too surely laid now." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-9.html)

---

## v. 28 — Horses from Egypt

**Enduring Word** sees this as "the sound of this dark note" — "This was in direct disobedience to Deuteronomy 17:16, which said to the kings of Israel: But he shall not multiply horses for himself, nor cause the people to return to Egypt to multiply horses." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-9/)

The Pulpit Commentary notes the parallel in 1 Kings 10:29 gives prices: a chariot from Egypt at 600 shekels of silver and a horse at 150 shekels. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-9.html)

---

## v. 29 — The Sources for Solomon's Acts

**Gill** notes this verse is "more largely expressed" than in Kings: "the acts of Solomon's reign were written in the book of Nathan the prophet, and in the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the visions of Iddo the seer." He notes the Septuagint and other versions read "concerning Jeroboam" rather than "against Jeroboam." The Pulpit Commentary notes that Ahijah and his work are clear from 1 Kings 11:28-40 and 14:1-20, and that the Chronicler "by a law omits any even reference to the defection of Solomon." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/9.htm; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-9.html)

---

## v. 30 — Forty-Year Reign

Enduring Word notes: "Many commentators believe that Solomon began his reign when he was about 20 years old. This means that Solomon did not live a particularly long life and the promise made in 1 Kings 3:14 was not fulfilled for Solomon, because of his disobedience." It quotes Clarke: "When we consider the excess in which he lived, and the criminal passions which he must have indulged among his thousand wives, and their idolatrous and impure worship, this life was as long as could be reasonably expected." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-9/)

---

## v. 31 — Solomon Rests with His Fathers

**Enduring Word** (Pentecostal/charismatic) offers a notably sober reflection: "This does not necessarily mean that Solomon died a saved man. It is a familiar phrase used in 1 and 2 Kings (used 25 times) and was used of such wicked kings as Ahab (1 Kings 22:40). It simply means that Solomon passed to the world beyond. We cannot say with certainty that he is in heaven." It quotes G. Campbell Morgan: "Yielding to certain lower things of his nature, he became a slave to them, and dragged down his nation with him... The story is perhaps one of the most striking illustrations of the fact that opportunity and privilege, even God bestowed, are not enough in themselves to assure full realisation." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-9/)

**Matthew Henry** (evangelical) takes a markedly different, more hopeful view: "It is very observable that no mention is here made of Solomon's departure from God in his latter days, not the least hint given of it... Because, though he fell, yet he was not utterly cast down. His sin is not again recorded, because it was repented of, and pardoned, and became as if it had never been. Scripture-silence sometimes speaks. I am willing to believe that its silence here concerning the sin of Solomon is an intimation that none of the sins he committed were mentioned against him (Ezek. 33:16). When God pardons sin he casts it behind his back and remembers it no more." Henry also suggests the Holy Ghost teaches us "not to take delight in repeating the faults and follies of others." (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC14009.HTM)

---

## Points of Difference Between Traditions

### Solomon's Eternal Destiny (v. 31)
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word):** Expresses uncertainty about whether Solomon died as a believer; "rested with his fathers" is a neutral phrase used even of wicked kings like Ahab.
- **Evangelical/Reformed (Matthew Henry):** Believes Solomon repented and was pardoned; the Chronicler's silence on his sins is a sign of divine forgiveness. (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC14009.HTM)

### The Queen of Sheba's Faith (v. 8)
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word, citing Dilday):** Her words were likely "polite recognition rather than genuine personal faith" — she returned home without evident conversion.
- **Evangelical (Matthew Henry):** Views her blessing of God more positively, as a model of giving thanks for the gifts of others.
- **Reformed (Ligonier):** Sees the visit as partial fulfillment of the Abrahamic promise that Israel would bless the nations, looking forward to Christ. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/solomons-accomplishments-and-renown)
- **Brethren/Typological (Grant):** Reads the queen as a "lovely picture of the great interest in the Lord Jesus that will be awakened among the Gentiles when He takes His kingdom." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/2-chronicles-9.html)

### Solomon's Wealth: Blessing or Danger?
- **Reformed (Ligonier):** Emphasises that "God is not opposed to richly blessing His people" and that great riches "are not inherently incompatible with faithful service." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/solomons-accomplishments-and-renown)
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word):** Emphasises the danger — Solomon's multiplying of gold and horses was direct disobedience to Deuteronomy 17, and the 666 connection signals a "good man corrupted." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-9/)
- **Precept Austin (citing John Olley, evangelical):** The Chronicler "provides a vision of what God intends for his people when they follow him wholeheartedly... with lasting blessing inseparable from loyal worship." It foreshadows Matthew 6:31–33 — "seek first the kingdom." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-9-commentary)

### The Number 666 (v. 13)
- **Enduring Word:** Draws an explicit typological link to the Antichrist in Revelation 13:18, suggesting the Antichrist may be "a good man corrupted" like Solomon. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-9/)
- **Traditional commentaries (Henry, Pulpit, Gill):** Do not make this connection; they simply discuss the monetary value of the gold.

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship / Historical-Critical

Precept Austin (citing Raymond Dillard) emphasises that **commercial motivations** likely underlay the queen's visit: "The economy of ancient Saba was built on trade in frankincense and myrrh. Access to sea trade through Tyre... required passage through Solomon's monopoly on the overland routes." Solomon's joint naval ventures with Hiram "may have been cutting into the queen's overland routes." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-9-commentary)

The Pulpit Commentary notes the debate over whether "ships of Tarshish" went to Spain (Tartessus) or Ophir, and whether voyages of three years involved circumnavigating Africa. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-9.html)

### Catholic / Orthodox

I was unable to fetch content from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org within the available tool limits. No specific Catholic or Orthodox commentary on 2 Chronicles 9 was retrieved.

### Prosperity / Word of Faith

No direct prosperity-gospel teaching on this chapter was found in the searched sites. However, the Reformed (Ligonier) caution is relevant: "While we should not serve God merely to secure material blessings, we should also not be ashamed when we are faithful to God and He blesses us materially."
